title_original: “Leica Hall of Fame” Prize : Graciela Iturbide
excerpt_original: She is the most famous contemporary Mexican photographer in the world: this year, Graciela Iturbide has been awarded the “Leica Hall of Fame” prize […] Cet article “Leica Hall of Fame” Prize : Graciela Iturbide est apparu en premier sur The Eye of Photography Magazine .

blocks.text: She is the most famous contemporary Mexican photographer in the world: this year, Graciela Iturbide has been awarded the “Leica Hall of Fame” prize for her entire body of work. The award ceremony took place as part of the “Celebration of Photography” on October 8, 2026 at Leica World in Wetzlar. The accompanying exhibition, presenting more than 50 photographs, will be on view at the Leica Gallery in Wetzlar until January 2027. Iturbide’s photograph “Na’ Lupe Pan,” from the series “Juchitán,” Oaxaca, Mexico, 1986, has been chosen as the “Leica Picture of the Year 2026.”

The exhibition offers an in-depth overview of the artist’s work, devoted mainly to Latin American cultural history. Exploring universal themes such as life and death, rituals and the experiences of everyday life, Iturbide’s visual universe is characterized by its moving poetry and magic. The photographer highlights the tensions between culture and nature, tradition and modernity, identity and representation, ensuring that her images retain an enigmatic ambiguity. Deeply rooted in Mexican indigenous culture and blending surrealist elements with religion and mysticism, Graciela Iturbide has developed, over many decades, an inimitable visual language – mainly in black and white. Birds and masks appear again and again as symbolic companions. The photographer’s best-known work, the astonishing “Nuestra Señora de las iguanas” (Our Lady of the Iguanas), was taken in 1979 in a market in Juchitán. It is a mysterious portrait of a female vendor wearing a crown of live iguanas: a Mexican hydra, but also, in the Christian interpretation, a female figure of Christ wearing a crown of thorns of an animal nature.

Graciela Iturbide’s photographic work belongs to a humanist tradition that incorporates psychological and spiritual elements, transforming the documentary image into a form of subjective photography of extraordinary richness and nuance. Besides her still lifes and landscapes, it is her social reportage on the living conditions of Mexico’s indigenous communities and on the importance of matriarchal social structures that caused a stir and established her as one of the most important photographic voices in Latin America.

The exhibition organized on the sidelines of the Leica Hall of Fame Award presentation brings together more than 50 photographs from five series: “Juchitán,” with pictures of this Mexican town in the state of Oaxaca (1979–1988), “México Clásicas” (1974–2008), “Pájaros” (Birds, 1987–1998), “Desierto de Sonora” (1979) and “Viajes” (Journeys), made in Ecuador, Panama, Argentina and Cuba (1972–1994).

Graciela Iturbide was born in Mexico City on May 16, 1942. Even as a child she was fascinated by photography: her father was a passionate amateur photographer. She married the architect Manuel Rocha Díaz (1936–1996) at the age of 19 and became the mother of three children. In 1969, she began studying film at the Universidad Nacional Autónoma de México (UNAM), at the Centro Universitario de Estudios Cinematográficos (CUEC). In 1970, she spent a year as an assistant to photographer Manuel Álvarez Bravo, whom she accompanied on many trips, discovering rural Mexico and the diversity of its indigenous communities. A stroke of fate, the death of her six-year-old daughter Claudia, radically upended Graciela Iturbide’s life, and she then chose to become a professional photographer. In 1975, she had her first exhibition in Mexico City, followed by her first in New York in 1976. From the 1980s onward, she began to gain international recognition. She has received numerous awards, including the W. Eugene Smith Grant (1987), the Hugo Erfurth Prize (1989), the Prix des Rencontres internationales de la photographie d’Arles (1991), the Hasselblad Award (2008), the gold medal of the Instituto Nacional de Bellas Artes y Literatura (INBAL) in Mexico City (2024) and the Princess of Asturias Award for the Arts (2025). Iturbide lives in Mexico City.
Leica Picture of the Year sold exclusively in Leica Galleries

An exclusive limited-edition photograph by Graciela Iturbide is available in Leica Galleries around the world as the “Leica Picture of the Year 2026.” The image, titled “Na’ Lupe Pan” and taken in Oaxaca, Mexico, in 1986, is part of the series “Juchitán.” Since 2021, Leica Camera AG has awarded the “Leica Picture of the Year” to exceptional Leica photographers who have been inducted into the Leica Hall of Fame. Following in the footsteps of Ralph Gibson, Thomas Hoepker, Elliott Erwitt, Herlinde Koelbl and Joel Meyerowitz, Graciela Iturbide is the photographer behind the 2026 “Leica Picture of the Year.”
The Leica Gallery in Paris (26 rue Boissy d’Anglas – 75008) will sell 3 prints starting in December 2026.

Images that have moved the world, moments that will remain forever engraved in memory: since 2011, Leica Camera AG has been inducting exceptional photographers into the Leica Hall of Fame – photographers whose view of the world made a difference and served as a vehicle for change. These emblematic images, now anchored in collective memory, bear witness to their work, touch the viewer and illustrate the “human condition” in a timeless way. Steve McCurry was the first to receive the Leica Hall of Fame Award in 2011, followed by Barbara Klemm, Nick Út, René Burri, Thomas Hoepker and Ara Güler. Joel Meyerowitz was honored in 2016, Gianni Berengo Gardin in 2017, then Bruce Davidson and Jürgen Schadeberg in 2018. Walter Vogel followed in 2019, Ralph Gibson in 2021, Elliott Erwitt in 2023 and Herlinde Koelbl in 2024. With the arrival of Graciela Iturbide, the number of members inducted into the Leica Hall of Fame now stands at 15.

At the “Celebration of Photography” held on October 8 at Leica World in Wetzlar, Graciela Iturbide’s induction into the Leica Hall of Fame was not the only highlight: the winners of the 46th Leica Oskar Barnack Award, as well as those of the LOBA Women Grant – awarded for the first time – were also honored. In addition, all the shortlisted series for LOBA 2026 are on display at the Ernst Leitz Museum until February 18, 2027.
